prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the cleanest case on this shortlist of a simple model with a sharp, falsifiable prediction that nature then confirmed. The Kane-Mele model (2005) identified the Z2 invariant and the protected helical edge states of the quantum spin Hall phase. Molenkamp's group measured the predicted quantized edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, so the theory and experiment loop is closed in one clear step. The concept, band topology and bulk-boundary correspondence rather than symmetry breaking, has spread through condensed matter, photonics, cold atoms and materials searches, and it has been confirmed for about twenty years by many groups on many platforms. The interpretation is stable, so recognition is not premature. After reconsidering my opening proposal I have moved Mele into the preferred trio in place of Hasan. If one asks who first identified the essential mechanism, Kane and Mele are inseparable. Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is important, but the 3D classification came from a wider group of theorists (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Roy) who are not on the credited list, and that makes the 3D credit harder to allocate cleanly than the 2D one.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the decisive HgTe proposal that told Molenkamp what to measure, and Zhang is deceased, so the narrative has a hole that no three-person citation fully closes. Dropping Hasan leaves the 3D topological insulator discovery, which is arguably the part with the broadest materials impact, unrecognized. The 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) also invites the objection that this is a continuation of an already honoured topic rather than a new one.

responses.point: Johansson ranked topological insulators only seventh because the Zhang death and the parallel contributions make the configuration hard, and because the 2016 prize overlap complicates novelty. He put circuit QED first.
responses.response: I take the credit problem seriously and it is why I changed my trio, but I disagree that the 2016 prize makes this redundant. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topology in the quantum Hall state and in phase transitions. The Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, with no external magnetic field, and its experimental realization in a real material are a distinct, later and experimentally verified discovery. Circuit QED, which you rank first, sits much closer to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so on novelty the overlap argument weighs more heavily against B038 than against B006.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators second behind twisted bilayer graphene. He argued that Mele is arguably inseparable from Kane for the theory and that the field is mature, so recognition would be timely or overdue.
responses.response: I agree on Mele, and I changed my preferred trio for that reason. Where we differ is the order. Twisted bilayer graphene is also a case of theory confirmed by experiment, but the superconducting pairing is still debated and the field is only about eight years old. I would not put it ahead of a field whose central claims have been checked on many platforms for two decades. I do think B017 is a strong second choice if the committee wants a younger topic.

responses.point: Olsson ranked topological insulators third. She values direct measurement of the key claims and said she would favour an experimental emphasis, while noting the list has four names and omits other theorists.
responses.response: I share the preference for direct measurement, and the HgTe transport experiment is the decisive one for the 2D phase. But a prize built on Molenkamp and Hasan alone would credit the confirmations without the idea that made them possible. Kane and Mele should stay, with Molenkamp as the experimental anchor. If the committee wants to keep Hasan, then I would want to see which theorist we give up, and I do not think the answer is Mele.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked topological insulators seventh. She noted it is outside her main field, that the prediction followed by decisive experiment is a model of fundamental discovery, and that the four-name list misses Zhang so credit is contested. She proposed Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: We end up on the same trio, and I think your point about the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit is the right framing. It argues for a citation that names the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation in HgTe, rather than a broad claim over all topological materials. I would still like to hear from the experimentalists whether the Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 ARPES work can be fitted in a way that does not push the count above three.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first because of the 1e-18 uncertainties, the tests of constants and relativistic geodesy, and the strong independent confirmation across many laboratories.
responses.response: The clock case is strong on maturity and attribution, since Katori and Ye form a natural pair. My reservation is conceptual. The advance is a very large gain in precision on an existing quantum-metrology idea, and the fundamental physics payoff so far consists of upper limits and a pending redefinition of the second. That is a major achievement, but I do not see it as opening a new class of phenomena the way topological insulators did. I would not object to it as a second part in a two-achievement prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a quantum spin Hall prize that omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and whether it is better to credit the 3D topological insulator discovery through Hasan instead of Mele.
How much weight the 2016 prize for topological phases should carry against a distinct, experimentally confirmed Z2 classification.
Whether a two-part prize with optical lattice clocks or twisted bilayer graphene would be preferable to a single topological insulator part.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known collaboration with any of the credited candidates, and my own research on turbulent aerosols and statistical physics is far from the topological insulator field. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, but no specific collaboration is known.
